first_impression.reaction: James's family want it in the church, I'm Anglican, and neither of us knew where to start, so I googled it. The first line reset my thinking in one go: 'A Greek Orthodox wedding is a sacrament, not a ceremony you write yourselves.' Then it tells me what to do first, which is see the priest before we hold anything. No 'fairytale', no 'dream day'. Calm, sure of itself, useful. Kept reading.

journey.quote: Before you hold a venue or send a save-the-date, sit down with your parish priest, check that the Church can marry you, and check that your date is open.
journey.reaction: This is the bit I needed. We were about to start shortlisting islands. Getting the order right saves us a wasted deposit and an awkward conversation with James's yiayia.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: The non-Orthodox partner must belong to a Christian denomination the Church accepts, for example Roman Catholic, Anglican, Uniting, Lutheran or Presbyterian.
journey.reaction: Relief. Anglican is on the list, so I'm not a problem. Straight answer, no hedging.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: A baptism performed by a female pastor or member of clergy is not accepted.
journey.reaction: Wait. My parish had a female rector when I was a baby, I honestly don't know who baptised me. Two paragraphs ago I was fine, now I might not be. The page states the rule and moves on without telling me what to do if that's me.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: If a minister from the other partner's church is close to you, they can be welcomed as a guest, or invited to speak at the reception.
journey.reaction: Thoughtful. Mum will want our family minister involved somehow, and this gives her a role instead of a no.

journey.section: Who can marry in the Greek Orthodox Church?
journey.quote: In families where the same godparent has baptised several cousins, that last rule is worth raising early.
journey.reaction: That's insider knowledge. I'd never have thought of it, and with James's family it's entirely possible.

journey.quote: In many Greek families the wedding sponsor is expected to baptise the first child, so choose with both roles in mind.
journey.reaction: Exactly the kind of thing that blows up in a family group chat later. Sending to James.

journey.section: Dates when weddings are not held
journey.quote: From 1 to 15 August, for the Dormition of the Theotokos.
journey.reaction: We'd half pencilled in August in Greece. Glad I saw this before anyone booked flights. Clear list, easy to screenshot.

journey.section: The Service of Betrothal and the rings
journey.quote: Tell your photographer, so they are watching the sponsor's hands and not waiting for the couple.
journey.reaction: Small, practical, the sort of thing only someone who's stood in the church would know. This is why I'd trust them with the rest of the day.

journey.section: The Greek Orthodox wedding ceremony, step by step
journey.quote: The priest blesses each of you with the rings three times, and the rings are placed on the fourth finger of the right hand.
journey.reaction: The step-by-step is clear and I can finally picture what my side of the family will be watching. Skimmed the readings and the cup, but I'd send this whole section to Mum and Dad so they're not lost on the day.

journey.section: Are there vows in a Greek Orthodox wedding?
journey.quote: If personal words matter to you, keep them for the reception.
journey.reaction: I did want to say something to James. This doesn't just say no, it gives me somewhere to put it. Good.

journey.quote: Its document steps run in a fixed order: each document except passports needs its own Apostille, then a Greek translation; copies go for approval at least four weeks before the date, approval for the Orthodox wedding coming from the Metropolis; and all documents must be issued within three months of the wedding date.
journey.reaction: This is the bit that matters most if we go to Greece, and it's one dense sentence about one hotel. I had to read it twice, and I'm a lawyer. I can't tell if this sequence applies everywhere or only at Elounda.

journey.quote: For any wedding in Greece, check with the Metropolis, the municipality and the Australian Embassy in Athens, including any fees.
journey.reaction: Same as the Santorini article: the Australian side is laid out cleanly, then the Greek side comes back to me as three offices to ring. 'Legal side sorted' is one of our three goals. I get that it varies, but I'd like to know who does that chasing.

journey.quote: On Paros, the municipality names Panagia Ekatontapiliani and a string of country chapels as favourite wedding churches, with guests arriving by boat, carriage or on foot with musicians.
journey.reaction: Now we're talking. Guests walking in with musicians is the opposite of a resort package. And the named resort chapels give me a real choice to talk through with James.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: Will the service be in Greek, or partly in English for guests?
journey.reaction: Half our guests won't understand a word of Greek. Useful list I'd actually take into the meeting with the priest.

journey.section: Plan your Greek Orthodox wedding with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: Your priest settles the service. Everything around it, from the island and the chapel to the guests' flights and the long lunch after, is ours to plan.
journey.reaction: Clean split of who does what. It answers my 'what does end-to-end actually mean' question for this kind of wedding, and it doesn't pretend they run the Church.

unanswered_questions: If I don't know whether a woman baptised me, how do we find out, and what happens if she did?
Is the Apostille, translation and approval sequence the same at every venue in Greece, or only at Elounda?
Have you planned a real Greek Orthodox wedding in Greece, with venue and date, that I can look at?
Which of the named chapels actually fit 60 to 90 guests inside, since the page doesn't say?
If we marry in Greece, does a parish priest in Australia still need to be involved, or does the Metropolis take it from there?
Can the service be partly in English anywhere, or is that up to each priest?
would_share_with: James (partner): the intro, the koumbaros and godparent point, and the closed dates
James's parents and yiayia: the step-by-step ceremony, to show we're taking it seriously
Mum and Dad (contributing): the non-Orthodox partner section and the line about our minister speaking at the reception

cta_reaction.quote: When your priest has confirmed the Church side, [book a Wedded Concierge consultation](https://weddedwonderland.com/wonderland-concierge?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=greek-orthodox-wedding&utm_content=primary) and plan the celebration around it.
cta_reaction.why: I like that it tells me to see the priest first. That's the opposite of hard-sell and it makes me trust the call more. The fee in writing and one point of contact speak to my two biggest fears. But I'd see the priest, read another post or two and want a real Orthodox wedding in Greece to look at before I enquire.

top_3_changes: In 'If one partner is not Orthodox', after 'A baptism performed by a female pastor or member of clergy is not accepted.', add one plain line on what to do next (for example, check who performed the baptism when you order the certificate, and raise it with the priest straight away), so a mixed-faith reader isn't left hanging on it.

In 'The church and the paperwork', break the long Elounda sentence into a short numbered sequence (Apostille, translation, approval four weeks ahead, issued within three months, register within 40 days) and say clearly whether it is that venue's process or the usual pattern in Greece.

In 'Who can marry in the Greek Orthodox Church?', move the 'For a wedding in Greece, the local Metropolis sets the requirements' point into a one-line signpost near the top of the article, so a couple who hasn't chosen Australia or Greece knows from the start which rules apply where.
